title: Oak end-grain serving board
subtitle: A small knife-friendly cutting and serving board in end-grain oak
excerpt: An end-grain oak serving board: 25 cm by 18 cm, 4 cm thick, with a juice groove routed around the perimeter and a hanging cord in the corner. Seasoned oak, card-scraper finish, danish-oil treatment. End grain is the traditional surface for butcher blocks: the blade enters between fibres rather than across them.

glossaryTerms.definition: Air-dried or kiln-dried wood at a stable moisture content for indoor use (8 to 12 per cent). Does not shrink after working.
The surface revealed when wood is cut across the grain direction, showing the cross-section of the annual rings.
A thin steel plate with a turned burr edge used to take very fine shavings from a wood surface, leaving a cleaner finish than sandpaper.

content.text: An end-grain board presents the cross-section of the wood to the working surface. When a knife blade falls on
end grain

, it parts the fibres longitudinally and they spring back; the surface self-heals to a degree that a long-grain surface does not. This is why professional butcher blocks are always end-grain. This project makes a smaller version in
seasoned
oak: a 25 cm by 18 cm slab cut from a 4 cm thick oak board, with the faces presenting end grain to the kitchen.

End-grain boards are only safe for food use if the finish is food-safe. Oak contains tannins that react with iron; do not use ferrous metal tools on oil-treated oak without wiping clean. Do not use boiled linseed oil: boiled linseed contains metallic driers and is not food-safe.
Wood

Seasoned oak from a 4 cm thick board. The board face is the long grain; the board end (the cut end of the board) is the end grain and is the working surface of the serving board. Cut a 25 cm by 18 cm section from the end of the board. The thickness of the board (4 cm) becomes the height of the serving board on the kitchen counter. Maple or beech in the same configuration are the alternatives: both are harder than oak and equally food-safe.
Tools
Smoothing plane No. 4 (optional): for flattening the end-grain surfaces before scraping.
Card scraper: for final levelling and smoothing of both faces.
Japanese waterstone, 1000 grit (optional): for keeping the plane iron sharp on dense oak.
Danish oil: food-safe penetrating finish for the working surface.
Method
Step 1: Flatten both faces

The sawn end-grain surface will be slightly rough from the saw. Flatten both faces with the smoothing plane, taking diagonal cuts across the face to prevent the plane following the grain lines. Then take one or two passes at 90 degrees to the first passes to confirm flatness. End grain is hard to plane without tear-out; a sharp iron at a slightly steeper pitch (30 degrees instead of 25) helps.
Step 2: Scrape to a smooth surface
Use the
card scraper

to take the surface to a fine, even finish. The scraper leaves a cleaner end-grain surface than sandpaper, which embeds grit into the open pores of oak. Work with the scraper at 75 to 80 degrees to the surface, pushing or pulling in the direction that produces a thin curl rather than dust.
Step 3: Chamfer the edges

Use a block plane or the card scraper to cut a 3 mm chamfer around all four long-grain edges of the board. The chamfer reduces the risk of the edge splitting in use and gives the board a clean, finished profile.
Step 4: Drill the hanging cord hole
Drill a 6 mm hole in one corner of the board, 15 mm from each edge. Thread a 30 cm loop of cotton twine through the hole and knot it. The board hangs from this loop when not in use.
Finishing

Apply danish oil to all surfaces including the long-grain sides. End grain absorbs oil fast; apply two coats to the end-grain faces, leaving the first coat to soak for thirty minutes before the second. Cure for five days before using with food. The cure time for danish oil is five to seven days regardless of the piece size.

attrs.symptom: The plane is tearing out chunks on the end grain
attrs.cause: The plane iron is not sharp enough for oak end grain, or the cutting angle is too low.
attrs.fix: Hone the iron to a mirror edge on the waterstone. If tear-out continues, tilt the iron to a higher bedding angle by adding a back-bevel with the waterstone.

attrs.symptom: The board split along the grain during drying after oiling
attrs.cause: The board was not fully seasoned when oiled; the danish oil sealed the surface and accelerated stress cracking.
attrs.fix: Only oil wood at stable moisture content (8 to 12 per cent). Check with a moisture meter if available.
